pos: n. / title (Christ's self-designation as the shepherd who lays down His life; rendering Greek ho poimen ho kalos)
etymology: Shepherd, Old English sceaphierde, sheep-herd. The Greek adjective is kalos, not agathos — good in the sense of beautiful, noble, fit for its purpose, the word used of a fine workman and a true coin.
biblical_def: Christ's self-designation in John 10: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (John 10:11), “I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine” (John 10:14). He sets Himself against the hireling, who “seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth… because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep” (John 10:12–13). The title fulfils Ezekiel's promise that God would shepherd the flock His shepherds had failed: “Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out” (Eze 34:11). Hebrews calls Him “that great shepherd of the sheep” (Heb 13:20) and Peter “the chief Shepherd” (1Pe 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shepherd as a man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the pasture; and, in a spiritual sense, a pastor, a minister of the gospel who superintends a church or congregation.
webster_full: SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the pasture.
2. A swain; a rural lover.
3. The pastor of a church; one who exercises the pastoral office.
THE GOOD SHEPHERD, the Savior, who is called the shepherd and bishop of souls.
scriptures: John 10:11
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
John 10:14
I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.
John 10:12
But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
For thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out.
Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
corruption_summary: The Good Shepherd is preached as gentleness only, and the definition He gives is a death.
corruption_paragraphs: The picture on the nursery wall is a young man with a lamb on his shoulders, and it is not wrong, but it is not the definition. Christ defines the title Himself, twice in four verses, and the definition is a corpse: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. The Greek adjective is kalos, not agathos — not morally good in the abstract but good at the work, fit for the purpose, the word for a craftsman who is genuinely a craftsman. What makes Him the good shepherd is not His tenderness but His competence at the one thing shepherding finally requires, which is dying between the flock and the wolf.

The contrast He draws is with the hireling, and it is a warning to ministers rather than a comfort to congregations. The hireling is not a wolf; he is a paid man doing real work, and he is exposed only when the wolf appears — at which point he flees, and the text gives the reason without softening it: because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep. A ministry can look identical to the true one for years and be distinguished only in the hour of cost. Ezekiel 34 is the same charge against the shepherds of Israel, who fed themselves and not the flock, and the LORD's answer there is not to reform them but to come Himself.

The last corruption is the softest: to keep the shepherd and lose the sheep. He says “I know my sheep, and am known of mine” and, in the same chapter, “ye believe not, because ye are not of my sheep” (John 10:26) — a sentence that reverses the order everyone expects. The flock is particular, given to Him by the Father, and He lays down His life for the sheep, not for the wolves and not for the world in general. That is the doctrine of particular redemption, and it is not a Calvinist gloss on the passage; it is the passage.
roots_summary: Greek poimen (G4166), shepherd; kalos (G2570), good, noble, fit; psuchen tithemi (G5087), to lay down one's life; misthotos (G3411), a hireling; Hebrew ro'eh (H7462), shepherd.
roots_lines: Greek poimen (G4166) — shepherd; John 10:11, 10:14, 10:16, Hebrews 13:20, 1 Peter 2:25; archipoimen (G750), chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:4.
Greek kalos (G2570) — good, noble, fit for purpose; John 10:11, 10:14, 10:32, 1 Timothy 4:6.
Hebrew ro'eh (H7462) — shepherd, to feed; Psalm 23:1, Ezekiel 34:2, 34:11–12, Isaiah 40:11.
usage: “The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” — the title defined by a death.
“He is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep” — the man exposed only when the wolf comes.
“I know my sheep, and am known of mine” — a particular flock, not a general goodwill.

pos: n. / title (Christ as the sustenance of the soul; rendering Greek ho artos tes zoes)
etymology: Bread, Old English bread; the Greek artos is the ordinary loaf. The title takes the plainest and most necessary food in the ancient world and makes it a name for a Person.
biblical_def: Christ's self-designation in John 6: “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst” (John 6:35); “I am that bread of life. Your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead” (John 6:48–49); “I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world” (John 6:51). The discourse stands on the manna — “he gave them bread from heaven to eat” (John 6:31) — and on the feeding of the five thousand, and it ends with most of the crowd walking away (John 6:66).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bread as food made of flour or meal; and, in Scripture, food in general, support of life, and spiritually the doctrine of the gospel and Christ Himself.
webster_full: BREAD, n. A mass of dough, made by moistening and kneading the flour or meal of some species of grain, and baked in an oven.
2. Food in general.
3. Support of life in general; maintenance.
BREAD OF LIFE, in a spiritual sense, Christ, the author and support of spiritual life.
scriptures: John 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
John 6:48
I am that bread of life.
John 6:51
I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.
John 6:53
Then Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you.
John 6:66
From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
John 6:31
Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat.
corruption_summary: The bread of life is read as the Supper, and the discourse was preached a year before the Supper existed.
corruption_paragraphs: John 6 is the passage on which the doctrine of the mass has most often been rested, and the chronology is against the reading. The discourse is preached in a synagogue at Capernaum, at passover time, a full year before the upper room; the crowd who heard it had no ordinance to refer it to, and could not have understood it of a rite that did not exist. The Lord Himself supplies the key at the end of the chapter, when the saying proves hard: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life” (John 6:63). The eating is believing, and He says so plainly in verse 35, where coming and believing stand in the two halves of one sentence.

That does not make the language mild. “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you” (John 6:53) is deliberately offensive to a people forbidden blood, and it emptied the room: from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. The Lord did not soften it or call them back; He turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away. A gospel arranged so that nobody ever walks away is not the gospel of John 6.

The manna is the argument's hinge and the corruption most often misses it. Your fathers did eat manna, and are dead — the miracle bread of the exodus, given daily for forty years, kept a nation alive and buried every one of them. What the crowd wanted was more of that: bread that solves today. Christ offers bread that solves death, and the difference between the two requests is the difference between the multitude who followed for the loaves and the disciple who says, Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life.
roots_summary: Greek artos (G740), bread, a loaf; zoe (G2222), life; trogo (G5176), to eat, chew; manna (G3131); Hebrew lechem (H3899), bread, food.
roots_lines: Greek ho artos tes zoes (G740, G2222) — the bread of life; John 6:35, 6:48; ho artos ho zon, the living bread, John 6:51.
Greek trogo (G5176) — to eat, chew; John 6:54, 6:56–58, the deliberately physical verb.
Hebrew man (H4478) — manna; Exodus 16:15, 16:31, Numbers 11:7, Joshua 5:12.
usage: “He that cometh to me shall never hunger” — coming and believing in one sentence.
“Your fathers did eat manna… and are dead” — bread that solves today against bread that solves death.
“From that time many of his disciples went back” — the sermon that emptied the room.

pos: n. phrase / title (the incarnation; the eternal Logos taking human nature; rendering Greek ho logos sarx egeneto)
etymology: Greek logos, word, reason, account; sarx, flesh, human nature in its weakness; egeneto, became, came to be. John chose the harshest available noun for humanity: not anthropos, man, but flesh.
biblical_def: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The One who became flesh is identified in the first verse: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and “all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made” (John 1:3). Paul describes the same act as a taking, not a ceasing: He “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Php 2:7). Hebrews gives the purpose: “forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death” (Heb 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incarnation as the act of assuming flesh, or of taking a human body and the nature of man; and the Word, in theology, as the second person in the Trinity, called also the Logos.
webster_full: INCARNATION, n. The act of assuming flesh, or of taking a human body and the nature of man.
2. The state of being incarnated.
WORD, n. In theology, the second person in the Trinity, called also the Logos.
In the beginning was the word, and the word was with God, and the word was God.
scriptures: John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
John 1:3
All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.
Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
Heb 2:14

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil;

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.
corruption_summary: The incarnation is described as God stopping being God for a while, and John's verb is became in the sense of taking on, not of laying down.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest error is a subtraction: that in becoming flesh the Son emptied Himself of deity, set aside omniscience and omnipotence, and lived as a man with the divine attributes suspended. Philippians 2:7 is the verse appealed to — He made himself of no reputation, literally emptied himself — and the sentence says what the emptying consisted of: and took upon him the form of a servant. The emptying is a taking. He added a nature; He did not subtract one, and John 1:14 keeps the deity in the same breath as the flesh, since it is precisely in the flesh that they beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father.

The opposite error is an addition of unreality: that the flesh was an appearance, a garment, a mode of manifestation — the old docetic instinct, which survives wherever the Lord's hunger, weariness, tears and dread are treated as a performance. John chose the word sarx to make that impossible. He does not say the Word became a man, which would have been true and gentler; he says the Word became flesh, the mortal, tired, hungry stuff, the word used for what is grass and withers. And the Gospel that opens so has Him asleep in a boat, thirsty at a well, and weeping at a grave.

The verb of dwelling carries the third point, and the English hides it. Eskenosen is to pitch a tent, from the noun for tabernacle; John is saying that the glory which filled the tent in the wilderness and then the temple has now taken up residence in a body. That is why the next clause is we beheld his glory — the Shekinah is being reported by eyewitnesses who ate with it. The incarnation is not a symbol of God's nearness. It is the nearness.
roots_summary: Greek logos (G3056), word; sarx (G4561), flesh; ginomai (G1096), to become; skenoo (G4637), to tabernacle, dwell in a tent; monogenes (G3439), only begotten.
roots_lines: Greek logos (G3056) — the Word; John 1:1, 1:14, 1 John 1:1, Revelation 19:13.
Greek skenoo (G4637) — to pitch a tent, dwell; John 1:14, Revelation 7:15, 21:3 — the tabernacle word.
Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten; John 1:14, 1:18, 3:16, 3:18, 1 John 4:9.
usage: “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” — the verb is to pitch a tent.
“Took upon him the form of a servant” — the emptying is a taking.
“We beheld his glory” — the Shekinah reported by eyewitnesses.

pos: n. / title (Christ's last self-designation in Scripture; rendering Greek ho aster ho lampros ho proinos)
etymology: The morning star is the planet Venus, the last light to rise before dawn and the sign that the night is nearly over. The image is fixed in Balaam's oracle of a Star out of Jacob.
biblical_def: The last self-designation the Lord gives in Scripture: “I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16). He promises the same to the overcomer at Thyatira: “and I will give him the morning star” (Rev 2:28). The image runs back to Balaam — “there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel” (Num 24:17) — and forward through Peter: “ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts” (2Pe 1:19). Malachi's parallel is the sunrise: “the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings” (Mal 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines morning star as the planet Venus, when it precedes the sun in rising; and day-star as the morning star, Lucifer, Venus, the star which precedes the morning light.
webster_full: MORNING-STAR, n. The planet Venus, when it precedes the sun in rising.
DAY-STAR, n. The morning star; the star which precedes the morning light.
scriptures: I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
Rev 2:28
And I will give him the morning star.

I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
Mal 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
corruption_summary: The title is confused with Lucifer's, and Isaiah's morning star is a fallen king while Revelation's is the Lord Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection is old and is still circulated: Isaiah 14:12 addresses one whom the Latin rendered Lucifer, son of the morning, and Revelation 22:16 has Christ call Himself the bright and morning star; therefore, it is said, the two are the same figure. They are not the same word and not the same claim. Isaiah's oracle is a taunt against the king of Babylon — the passage names him in verse 4 — whose pride said, I will ascend into heaven, and whose fall is the point; the epithet is a description of a brief brightness that was extinguished, and the Latin translators' choice of Lucifer, light-bearer, is a translation, not a name. The morning star of Revelation rises and does not set.

The pastoral force of the title is in its timing, and it is easy to miss. The morning star is not the dawn; it is the last light of the night and the promise that the dawn is coming. Peter puts the Christian in exactly that hour: a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn and the day star arise in your hearts. The church lives in the interval, with a sure word of prophecy and no daylight yet, and the title is given to a people who are being told to hold on.

The last line of the Bible's last self-designation places two things side by side: the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star. He is David's origin and David's descendant at once, which is the paradox the Lord had already put to the Pharisees from Psalm 110 — if David call him Lord, how is he his son? A title that holds both ends of that is not a decoration on the end of the book; it is the summary of it.
roots_summary: Greek aster (G792), star; lampros (G2986), bright; proinos (G4407), of the morning; phosphoros (G5459), day star, light-bringer; Hebrew kokab (H3556), star.
roots_lines: Greek ho aster ho lampros ho proinos (G792, G2986, G4407) — the bright and morning star; Revelation 22:16, and Revelation 2:28.
Greek phosphoros (G5459) — day star, light-bringer; 2 Peter 1:19 only.
Hebrew kokab (H3556) — star; Numbers 24:17; and helel (H1966), Isaiah 14:12, of the king of Babylon.
usage: “I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” — the last self-designation in Scripture.
“Until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts” — the church's hour is before dawn.
“There shall come a Star out of Jacob” — Balaam's oracle, spoken for hire and true.

pos: n. / title (Christ as the healer of soul and body; from His own comparison in Matthew 9:12)
etymology: Physician, Greek iatros, one who heals. The title is not a formula of Scripture but a summary of Christ's own comparison, and of the covenant name given at Marah, Jehovah-rapha, the LORD that healeth thee.
biblical_def: The title comes from His own defence of the company He kept: “They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick… for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Mat 9:12–13; Mar 2:17; Luk 5:31–32). It rests on the covenant name at Marah: “I am the LORD that healeth thee” (Exo 15:26), and on the psalm that pairs the two cures: “Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases” (Psa 103:3). Jeremiah's question is the ache the title answers: “Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?” (Jer 8:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines physician as a person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies for diseases; and, figuratively, one that heals or corrects moral disease.
webster_full: PHYSICIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies for diseases.
2. One that heals or corrects moral disease.
scriptures: Mat 9:12
But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
Mat 9:13
But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

And said, If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee.
Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases;
Jer 8:22
Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?
corruption_summary: The Great Physician is invoked chiefly for bodies, and the sentence He said it in is about who He came to call.
corruption_paragraphs: The title is nearly always quoted at a sickbed, and that use is not wrong — He healed bodies constantly and without charge. But He coined the comparison at a dinner table, surrounded by publicans and sinners, with the Pharisees asking His disciples why their Master ate with such people; and the sentence finishes with the diagnosis: I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. The illness in view is sin, the patients are the disreputable, and the people excluded are not the wicked but the well — those who believe they are already whole.

That makes the title a hard one, because a physician is of no use to a man who denies he is ill, and the Pharisees are not caricatures. They were the most careful, most orthodox, most self-denying men in the country. Their disqualification was a single conviction: that they were whole. The modern equivalents are easy to find and uncomfortable to name, and every church contains people who would be scandalised by the guest list at that table and who have never once been to the doctor.

Psalm 103:3 keeps the two cures in the right order and refuses to separate them: who forgiveth all thine iniquities, who healeth all thy diseases. The forgiveness is first and is promised without qualification; the healing is real and, in this age, partial — Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick and told Timothy to take wine for his stomach. A gospel that promises the second unconditionally and mislays the first has the physician's business exactly backwards, and it breaks on the first funeral.
roots_summary: Greek iatros (G2395), physician; ischuo (G2480), to be strong, whole; kakos echo, to be ill; Hebrew rapha (H7495), to heal; Jehovah-rapha, the LORD that healeth.
roots_lines: Greek iatros (G2395) — physician; Matthew 9:12, Mark 2:17, 5:26, Luke 4:23, 5:31, Colossians 4:14 of Luke.
Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, cure; Exodus 15:26, Psalm 103:3, 147:3, Isaiah 53:5, Jeremiah 8:22.
Hebrew tsori (H6875) — balm; Jeremiah 8:22, 46:11, Genesis 37:25.
usage: “They that be whole need not a physician” — said at a table full of publicans.
“I am the LORD that healeth thee” — the covenant name at Marah.
“Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases” — the order matters.

pos: n. / title (Christ as the only lawful entrance to the fold and to salvation; rendering Greek he thura ton probaton)
etymology: Door, Old English duru; Greek thura. In an eastern sheepfold the shepherd often lay across the opening at night, so that the door was a body.
biblical_def: “Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep” (John 10:7); “I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture” (John 10:9). He contrasts every other approach: “He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). The exclusivity is repeated four chapters later — “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (John 14:6) — and by Peter before the council: “neither is there salvation in any other” (Act 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines door as an opening or passage into a house or apartment; the frame of boards that shuts such an opening; and, figuratively, entrance, means of approach or access.
webster_full: DOOR, n. An opening or passage into a house, or other building, or into any room, apartment or closet, by which persons enter.
2. The frame of boards, or any piece of board or plank that shuts such an opening.
3. Entrance; as the door of life.
4. Avenue; means of approach or access.
scriptures: John 10:7
Then said Jesus unto them again, Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep.
John 10:9
I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture.
John 10:1
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
John 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
corruption_summary: Many doors are proposed and Christ called Himself the door, with everyone climbing in another way a thief.
corruption_paragraphs: “I am the door” is one of the least negotiable sentences in Scripture, because a door is not a preference among routes; it is the opening in a wall, and where there is one door there is no second. The Lord makes the exclusion explicit rather than leaving it to inference: he that entereth not by the door, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber. The alternatives are not described as sincere paths up the same mountain but as burglary. That is offensive in every age and was designed to be.

The corruption in the church is subtler than pluralism and more common: additional doors of its own manufacture — a rite, a party, an experience, a standard of respectability, without which a man is not quite let in. Every such requirement is a second entrance cut in a wall that has one, and John 10:9 is the answer to it: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved. Any man, and the only qualification named is entering.

The second half of the promise is usually dropped and is the tender part: he shall go in and out, and find pasture. The door is not a turnstile admitting a man once to a locked enclosure; it is the ordinary movement of a flock, out to feed in the morning and in to safety at night, both directions through the same Person. Salvation in this figure is not merely getting in. It is a life with a door in it that is always open the right way.
roots_summary: Greek thura (G2374), door; aule (G833), fold, court; sozo (G4982), to save; nome (G3542), pasture; lestes (G3027), robber.
roots_lines: Greek thura (G2374) — door; John 10:1, 10:2, 10:7, 10:9, Revelation 3:20, 4:1.
Greek aule (G833) — sheepfold, court; John 10:1, 10:16.
Greek nome (G3542) — pasture; John 10:9, and 2 Timothy 2:17 of a canker spreading.
usage: “I am the door of the sheep” — an opening in a wall, and there is one.
“Climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief” — the alternatives named as burglary.
“Shall go in and out, and find pasture” — the half that is usually dropped.

pos: v. phrase (the believer's continuance in Christ as a branch in the stock; rendering Greek meno en emoi)
etymology: Abide, Old English abīdan, to wait, remain; the Greek meno is to stay, to lodge, to keep on remaining. The vine is Israel's oldest self-image, and the Lord takes it over in the upper room.
biblical_def: “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me” (John 15:4); “I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5). The alternative is stated without softening: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered” (John 15:6). The promise attached is prayer: “If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you” (John 15:7). Israel had been the vine that failed (Isa 5:1–7; Psa 80:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abide as to rest, or dwell; to continue permanently or in the same state; to remain, to be firm and immovable.
webster_full: ABIDE, v.i. To rest, or dwell.
2. To tarry or stay for a short time.
3. To continue permanently or in the same state; to be firm and immovable.
4. To remain, to continue.
scriptures: John 15:4
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
John 15:6
If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.
John 15:7
If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.
John 15:16

Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
corruption_summary: Abiding is made a mood to be maintained, and the figure is a branch that is either joined to the stock or is firewood.
corruption_paragraphs: Abiding has become one of the vaguest words in devotional English — a warm interior condition, achieved by quiet mornings and lost by busy ones, so that the Christian spends his life trying to get back into a feeling. The Greek is meno, to stay put, and the figure is horticultural rather than emotional. A branch does not abide by concentrating; it abides by not being cut off, and its abiding is visible in exactly one way, which the passage names four times: fruit. Verse 7 adds the second evidence, that His words abide in the disciple, which is a matter of what he knows and obeys rather than what he feels.

The clause everyone quotes is without me ye can do nothing, and it is usually softened to mean that things go better with prayer. The sentence has no such margin. A severed branch does not underperform; it dies, and its most vigorous appearance is the last of the sap it took with it. That is the doctrine of dependence at its sharpest, and it is spoken to apostles on the night before the crucifixion — men about to do more than any Christians since, and told in advance that their capacity was zero.

Verse 6 is the hard one and has been read as a threat of losing salvation. The chapter's own answer is verse 16: ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain — the same verb, meno. The branch that is taken away is the branch that never had life in it, the professing attachment with no sap crossing the join; Judas had left the room a few verses earlier, and the disciples had watched a branch be removed.
roots_summary: Greek meno (G3306), to remain, abide, continue; ampelos (G288), vine; klema (G2814), branch; karpos (G2590), fruit; kathairo (G2508), to purge, prune.
roots_lines: Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; John 15:4–7, 15:9–10, 15:16, 1 John 2:6, 2:28, 3:24.
Greek ampelos (G288) — vine; John 15:1, 15:4–5, Revelation 14:18; klema (G2814), branch; John 15:2, 15:4–6.
Greek kathairo (G2508) — to prune, purge; John 15:2, with the wordplay on katharoi, clean, in 15:3.
usage: “As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself” — cannot, not merely will not.
“Without me ye can do nothing” — said to apostles, the night before the cross.
“That your fruit should remain” — the same verb as abide.

pos: n. phrase (the burden Christ lays on His disciples, set against the burden of the law-teachers; rendering Greek ho zugos mou chrestos)
etymology: Yoke, Old English geoc, the wooden bar joining two oxen. The Greek chrestos is not easy in the sense of light but kindly, serviceable, well-fitting — the word used of good wine and of the kindness of God.
biblical_def: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Mat 11:28–30). The contrast is with the yoke the scribes laid on: “they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers” (Mat 23:4), and with the yoke Peter refused to lay on the Gentiles, “which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear” (Act 15:10). John states the principle: “his commandments are not grievous” (1Jn 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines yoke as a piece of timber, hollowed or made curving near each end, and fitted with bows for receiving the necks of oxen; and figuratively a mark of servitude, slavery, bondage, or a chain, a link, a bond of connection.
webster_full: YOKE, n. A piece of timber, hollowed or made curving near each end, and fitted with bows for receiving the necks of oxen; by which means two are connected for drawing.
2. A mark of servitude; slavery; bondage.
3. A chain; a link; a bond of connection; as the yoke of marriage.
4. A couple; a pair; as a yoke of oxen.
scriptures: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
Mat 23:4
For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.
Now therefore why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous.
corruption_summary: The easy yoke is offered as a life without demands, and a yoke is a working harness for two.
corruption_paragraphs: The invitation is read as an offer of ease, and the object offered is a yoke — a piece of shaped timber that goes on the neck of a working animal. Christ does not promise the removal of labour; He promises a different harness and a different Master, and the verbs He uses are take and learn. The rest is real and it is found in the pulling. Every reading that turns the passage into a promise of an undemanding Christianity has to explain why the Lord chose the one image in the ancient world that meant work.

The Greek word behind easy is chrestos, which means kindly, serviceable, well-fitting; it is used of wine that has mellowed and of the goodness of God that leadeth to repentance. A yoke that is chrestos is one that has been shaped to the shoulders and does not gall. The contrast is not between a heavy burden and no burden but between a yoke that fits and the yoke of Matthew 23:4 — burdens grievous to be borne, laid on other men's shoulders by teachers who would not touch them with a finger. The difference is the Maker, who wore one first.

There is a mirror-corruption inside the Reformed world, where the fear of cheap grace produces a Christianity that is all burden and no rest, and the man who has come labouring and heavy laden is handed a longer list. First John 5:3 stands against it as flatly as Matthew 23 stands against the other: this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous. Both errors misjudge the same word. The commandments are not light because little is asked; they are not grievous because the One who asks is meek and lowly and is pulling in the next bow.
roots_summary: Greek zugos (G2218), yoke; chrestos (G5543), kind, serviceable, easy; phortion (G5413), a burden, load; anapauo (G373), to give rest; barus (G926), heavy, grievous.
roots_lines: Greek zugos (G2218) — yoke; Matthew 11:29–30, Acts 15:10, Galatians 5:1, 1 Timothy 6:1.
Greek chrestos (G5543) — kind, gracious, easy; Matthew 11:30, Luke 5:39, 6:35, Romans 2:4, Ephesians 4:32.
Greek anapauo (G373) — to give rest; Matthew 11:28, and anapausis (G372), rest, Matthew 11:29.
usage: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me” — the object offered is a working harness.
“They bind heavy burdens… and will not move them with one of their fingers” — the yoke it is set against.
“His commandments are not grievous” — against the opposite error.

pos: n. phrase (the blood of Christ as that which ratifies the new covenant; rendering Greek to haima mou tes kaines diathekes)
etymology: Covenant, Latin convenire, to come together; the Greek diatheke is a disposition or testament, which is why Hebrews can argue from the law of wills. A covenant in the ancient world was cut, and the cutting was in blood.
biblical_def: At the table: “this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Mat 26:28); “This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many” (Mar 14:24); “This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you” (Luk 22:20; 1Co 11:25). The words are Moses' words at Sinai, deliberately taken up: “Behold the blood of the covenant, which the LORD hath made with you” (Exo 24:8), quoted in Hebrews 9:20. The new covenant itself was promised by Jeremiah: “I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel… I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jer 31:31–34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines covenant as a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons; and, in theology, the covenant of grace, in which God engages to bestow salvation on man upon the condition that man shall believe in Christ and yield obedience to the terms of the gospel.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
2. A writing containing the terms of agreement or contract between parties.
3. In theology, the covenant of works is that implied in the commands, prohibitions, and promises of God; the covenant of redemption is the mutual agreement between the Father and Son.
4. In church affairs, a solemn agreement between the members of a church.
scriptures: For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.
Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.
Exo 24:8
And Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, Behold the blood of the covenant, which the LORD hath made with you concerning all these words.
Heb 9:20
Saying, This is the blood of the testament which God hath enjoined unto you.
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: The cup is called a symbol of fellowship, and the Lord called it the blood of a covenant shed for the remission of sins.
corruption_paragraphs: What the Lord said over the cup was not a new metaphor but a quotation. Moses, having read the book of the covenant to the people, sprinkled them and said, Behold the blood of the covenant which the LORD hath made with you — and every man at that table had heard the sentence since childhood. Christ takes the formula, changes one word, and applies it to Himself: this is my blood of the new testament. The claim is enormous and was made quietly at supper: the covenant at Sinai is being superseded, and the ratifying blood this time is His own.

The clause most often dropped in modern communion services is the last one: for the remission of sins. Where it goes, the Supper drifts into a fellowship meal, a memorial of a good man, an expression of the congregation's togetherness — all of which are true of it and none of which is why the blood was shed. Hebrews states the principle the whole sacrificial system rested on: without shedding of blood is no remission (Heb 9:22). The cup is not primarily about the church's unity with itself; it is about a debt discharged.

The opposite corruption re-sheds the blood, offering the cup as a fresh propitiation at each celebration. Luke's own word forbids it: this cup is the new testament in my blood — the cup is the covenant document, not the payment repeated. Jeremiah's promise, which the Lord was invoking, ends with the sentence that settles it: I will remember their sin no more. A covenant whose terms include divine forgetfulness is not one that needs renewing every Sunday; it needs remembering, which is exactly what He told them to do.
roots_summary: Greek diatheke (G1242), covenant, testament; haima (G129), blood; ekcheo (G1632), to shed, pour out; aphesis (G859), remission; Hebrew berith (H1285), covenant.
roots_lines: Greek diatheke (G1242) — covenant, testament; Matthew 26:28, Luke 22:20, 1 Corinthians 11:25, Hebrews 8:8, 9:15–20.
Greek aphesis (G859) — remission, forgiveness; Matthew 26:28, Hebrews 9:22, 10:18, Acts 2:38.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; Exodus 24:8, Jeremiah 31:31–33, Genesis 15:18.
usage: “This is my blood of the new testament” — Moses' sentence with one word changed.
“For the remission of sins” — the clause most often dropped.
“I will remember their sin no more” — the covenant He was invoking.

pos: n. phrase (Christ's body given in death, as declared over the bread at the Supper; rendering Greek to soma to huper humon klomenon)
etymology: Broken, Old English brecan. The Greek klao is the ordinary verb for breaking bread, and the Authorized Version keeps the reading broken for you in Paul's account of the institution.
biblical_def: “And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24); “This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me” (Luk 22:19). The breaking of the bread is the sign, and the communion is real: “The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16). Isaiah had said what would be done to that body: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isa 53:5). And John records what was not done to it: “A bone of him shall not be broken” (John 19:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines break as to part or divide by force and violence; to burst; to rend apart; and, in the sacrament, the breaking of bread as the memorial of Christ's body.
webster_full: BREAK, v.t. To part or divide by force and violence, as a solid substance.
2. To burst or open by force.
3. To rend; to tear; to part by piercing or penetrating.
4. To crush; to shatter.
BREAKING OF BREAD, in Scripture, the celebration of the Lord's supper.
scriptures: And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
John 19:36
For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken.
corruption_summary: The broken body is treated as a picture only, and the same Scripture that says broken for you says a bone of him shall not be broken.
corruption_paragraphs: Two sentences sit close together in the New Testament and look like a contradiction. Paul records the Lord saying this is my body, which is broken for you; John records that the soldiers, finding Him already dead, brake not his legs, and says it happened that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken. Both are exact and neither yields. The body was broken in every way a body can be — scourged, pierced, bruised for our iniquities — and the passover lamb's one structural requirement was kept to the letter, so that the sign and the substance agreed even in the manner of the death. What was broken was the man; what was not broken was the lamb.

The corruption on one side makes the bread the body in substance, so that the breaking is a re-breaking; the corruption on the other empties it entirely, so that the bread is a visual aid and the table a lecture with props. First Corinthians 10:16 refuses both by calling it a communion of the body of Christ — a real participation, in which believing receivers feed spiritually on a Christ who is bodily in heaven and truly given to them by the Spirit. The Confession's phrase is that they receive and feed upon Christ crucified, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually.

The most neglected word in the sentence is for you. The breaking is not presented as a fact to be admired at a distance but as a transaction with a beneficiary named, and the command that follows is not to analyse it but to remember: this do in remembrance of me. Paul adds the warning that a man may eat unworthily and be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, which would be an extravagant thing to say about a symbol and is a sober thing to say about a communion.
roots_summary: Greek klao (G2806), to break, of bread; soma (G4983), body; koinonia (G2842), communion, participation; anamnesis (G364), remembrance; suntribo (G4937), to break in pieces.
roots_lines: Greek klao (G2806) — to break bread; 1 Corinthians 11:24, 10:16, Matthew 26:26, Acts 2:46, 20:7.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — communion, participation; 1 Corinthians 10:16, 1:9, 2 Corinthians 13:14.
Greek suntribo (G4937) — to break in pieces; John 19:36, quoting Exodus 12:46, Psalm 34:20.
usage: “This is my body, which is broken for you” — a transaction with a beneficiary named.
“A bone of him shall not be broken” — the lamb's one requirement, kept.
“The communion of the body of Christ” — more than a symbol, less than a substance.
